source_text: Διὰ τοῦτο οὐκ αὐτὴ μόνη τοιαύτη, ἀλλὰ καὶ αἱ λοιπαὶ πᾶσαι. Καὶ γὰρ περὶ Περσίδος τινός φησιν, Ἥτις πολλὰ ἐκοπίασεν εἰς ἡμᾶς, καὶ Μαρίαν καὶ Τρύφαιναν ἀπὸ τούτων θαυμάζει τῶν πόνων, ὅτι ἐκοπίων μετὰ τῶν ἀποστόλων, καὶ πρὸς τοὺς αὐτοὺς ἀγῶνας ἀπεδύσαντο. Καὶ πῶς Τιμοθέῳ γράφων φησὶ, Γυναικὶ δὲ διδάσκειν οὐκ ἐπιτρέπω, οὐδὲ αὐθεντεῖν τοῦ ἀνδρός; Ὅταν καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ εὐλαβὴς ᾖ, καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν πίστιν κεκτημένος, καὶ τῆς αὐτῆς σοφίας μετέχων· ὅταν δὲ ἄπιστος ᾖ καὶ πεπλανημένος, οὐκ ἀποστερεῖ τὴν αὐθεντίαν τῆς διδασκαλίας αὐτήν. Κορινθίοις γοῦν ἐπιστέλλων λέγει· Καὶ γυνὴ ἥτις ἔχει ἄνδρα ἄπιστον, μὴ ἀφιέτω αὐτόν. Τί γὰρ οἶδας, γύναι, εἰ τὸν ἄνδρα σώσεις; Πῶς δὲ ἂν ἔσωσεν ἡ πιστὴ γυνὴ τὸν ἄνδρα τὸν ἄπιστον; Κατηχοῦσα δηλονότι καὶ διδάσκουσα καὶ ἐνάγουσα πρὸς τὴν πίστιν, ὥσπερ οὖν καὶ αὕτη Ἀπολλὼ ἡ Πρίσκιλλα. Ἄλλως δὲ, ὅταν λέγῃ, Γυναικὶ διδάσκειν οὐκ ἐπιτρέπω, περὶ τῆς ἐν τῷ βήματι διδασκαλίας λέγει, περὶ τῆς ἐν κοινῷ διαλέξεως, καὶ τῆς κατὰ τὸν ἱερωσύνης λόγον· ἰδίᾳ δὲ παραινεῖν καὶ συμβουλεύειν οὐκ ἐκώλυσεν. Οὐ γὰρ ἂν, εἰ κεκωλυμένον ἦν, ταύτην ἐπῄνεσε τοῦτο ποιοῦσαν. δʹ. Ἀκουέτωσαν ἄνδρες, ἀκουέτωσαν ταῦτα καὶ γυναῖκες· ἐκεῖναι μὲν, ἵνα τὴν ὁμόφυλον καὶ συγγενῆ μιμήσωνται· οὗτοι δὲ, ἵνα μὴ γυναικὸς ἀσθενέστεροι φαίνωνται. Τίνα γὰρ ἕξομεν ἀπολογίαν, τίνα συγγνώμην, ὅταν γυναικῶν τοσαύτην προθυμίαν ἐπιδεικνυμένων καὶ τοσαύτην φιλοσοφίαν, ἡμεῖς τοῖς τοῦ κόσμου πράγμασιν ὦμεν συνδεδεμένοι διηνεκῶς; Ταῦτα καὶ ἄρχοντες μανθανέτωσαν, καὶ ἀρχόμενοι, καὶ ἱερεῖς, καὶ οἱ τῶν λαϊκῶν τὴν τάξιν ἔχοντες, ἵν' ἐκεῖνοι μὲν μὴ τοὺς πλουτοῦντας θαυμάζωσι, μηδὲ τὰς περιφανεῖς διώκωσιν οἰκίας, ἀλλ' ἀρετὴν μετὰ πενίας ζητῶσι, καὶ τοῖς πτωχοτέροις τῶν ἀδελφῶν μὴ ἐπαισχύνωνται, μηδὲ τὸν σκηνοποιὸν, καὶ τὸν βυρσοδέψην, καὶ τὸν πορφυροπώλην, καὶ τὸν χαλκοτύπον παρατρέχοντες, τοὺς ἐν δυναστείαις θεραπεύσωσιν· οἱ δὲ ἀρχόμενοι, ἵνα μὴ νομίζωσιν εἶναι κώλυμα πρὸς τὴν ὑποδοχὴν τῶν ἁγίων, ἀλλ' ἐννοοῦντες τὴν χήραν, ἢ τὸν Ἠλίαν ὑπεδέξατο, δράκα ἀλεύρου μόνον ἔχουσα, καὶ τούτους, οἳ τὸν Παῦλον διετίαν ἐξένισαν, τὰς οἰκίας διανοίγωσι τοῖς δεομένοις, καὶ πάντα τοῖς ξένοις ὦσι κοινὰ κεκτημένοι. Μὴ γάρ μοι τοῦτο εἴπῃς, ὅτι οἰκέτας οὐκ ἔχεις διακονουμένους. Κἂν γὰρ μυρίους ἔχῃς, ὁ Θεός σε κελεύει διὰ σαυτοῦ τῆς φιλοξενίας τὸν καρπὸν τρυγᾷν. Διὰ τοῦτο Παῦλος χήρᾳ γυναικὶ διαλεγόμενος, καὶ κελεύων αὐτὴν ξενοδοχεῖν, οὐ δι' ἑτέρων, ἀλλὰ δι' ἑαυτῆς τοῦτο ἐπέταττεν. Εἰπὼν γὰρ, Εἰ ἐξενοδόχησεν, ἐπήγαγεν, Εἰ ἁγίων πόδας ἔνιψεν. Οὐκ εἶπεν, εἰ χρήματα ἐδαπάνησεν, οὐδὲ, εἰ τοῖς οἰκέταις ἐκέλευσε τοῦτο ποιῆσαι, ἀλλ', εἰ δι' ἑαυτῆς τοῦτο εἰργάσατο. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ Ἀβραὰμ τριακοσίους ὀκτὼ καὶ δέκα οἰκογενεῖς ἔχων, αὐτὸς ἐπὶ τὴν ἀγέλην ἔτρεχε, καὶ τὸν μόσχον ἐβάσταζε, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ἅπαντα διηκόνει, καὶ τὴν γυναῖκα κοινωνὸν ἐποίει τῶν τῆς φιλοξενίας καρπῶν. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς καὶ ἐν φάτνῃ τίκτεται, καὶ ἐν οἰκίᾳ τικτόμενος τρέφεται, καὶ αὐξηθεὶς οὐκ εἶχε ποῦ τὴν κεφαλὴν κλίνῃ, ἵνα σε παιδεύσῃ διὰ πάντων μὴ πρὸς τὰ λαμπρὰ τοῦ βίου τούτου κεχηνέναι πράγματα, ἀλλ' εὐτελείας εἶναι ἐραστὴν πανταχοῦ, καὶ πτωχείαν διώκειν, καὶ περιουσίαν φεύγειν, καὶ ἔσωθεν καλλωπίζεσθαι.
thought_title: Women's teaching and the honor of hospitality
orientation: Chrysostom is explaining why Paul praised women like Priscilla for their labor, and is now answering an objection about Paul's command that women not teach.
pass_a_gloss: Because of this not she alone is such, but also all the rest. For indeed about a certain Persis he says, 'Who labored much among us,' and Mary and Tryphaena he admires from these labors, because they labored with the apostles, and stripped for the same contests. And how, writing to Timothy, does he say, 'But I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to have authority over a man'? When the husband is reverent, and possessing the same faith, and sharing the same wisdom; but when he is faithless and led astray, he does not deprive her of the authority of teaching. To the Corinthians at any rate, writing, he says: 'And a woman who has a faithless husband, let her not leave him. For what do you know, woman, whether you will save the husband?' But how would the believing woman save the faithless husband? By instructing clearly and teaching and leading him toward the faith, just as indeed this Priscilla did Apollos. But otherwise, when he says, 'I do not permit a woman to teach,' he speaks about the teaching on the platform, about the public discourse, and about the word according to the priesthood; but to advise and counsel privately he did not forbid. For he would not, if it had been forbidden, have praised this woman doing this. 4. Let men hear, let women hear these things; those women, in order that they may imitate the one of the same race and kin; these men, in order that they may not appear weaker than a woman. For what defense will we have, what pardon, when women display so much eagerness and so much discipline, but we are bound to the affairs of the world continually? Let rulers learn these things, and subjects, and priests, and those having the rank of the laity, in order that those rulers may not admire the rich, nor pursue conspicuous houses, but seek virtue with poverty, and not be ashamed of the poorer of the brothers, nor passing by the tentmaker, and the tanner, and the purple-seller, and the bronze-worker, serve those in positions of power; and the subjects, in order that they may not think it is a hindrance to the reception of the holy ones, but considering the widow, or Elijah whom she received, having only a handful of flour, and those who hosted Paul for two years, may open their houses to those in need, and may have all things held in common for strangers. For do not say this to me, that you do not have servants ministering. For even if you have ten thousand, God commands you to harvest the fruit of hospitality through yourself. Because of this Paul, conversing with a widow woman, and commanding her to host strangers, not through others, but through herself he commanded this. For having said, 'If she hosted strangers,' he added, 'If she washed the feet of the holy ones.' He did not say, if she spent money, nor, if she commanded the servants to do this, but, if through herself she worked this. Because of this also Abraham, having three hundred eighteen homeborn servants, himself ran to the herd, and carried the calf, and ministered all the other things, and made his wife a sharer of the fruits of hospitality. Because of this also our Lord Jesus Christ is born in a manger, and being born in a house is nourished, and having grown did not have where to lay the head, in order that he may teach you through all things not to gape at the splendid affairs of this life, but to be a lover of frugality everywhere, and to pursue poverty, and to flee abundance, and to be adorned within.

choices.why: The verb means to strip off clothing, used metaphorically for athletes preparing for a contest; 'stripped for' preserves the athletic image of the contests (ἀγῶνας) that follows.
The noun αὐθεντία is the cognate of the verb αὐθεντεῖν just quoted from 1 Timothy; keeping 'authority' preserves the echo of the Pauline text Chrysostom is discussing.
βῆμα is the raised platform for public speaking; 'platform' conveys the public, official setting Chrysostom contrasts with private counsel.
Per the glossary, φιλοσοφία here means the Christian ascetic way of life, not philosophy in the modern sense.
The verb means to open the mouth wide in wonder or desire; 'gape at' preserves the vivid, slightly contemptuous image of longing for worldly splendor.
περιουσία means surplus wealth or abundance; 'abundance' contrasts naturally with the poverty (πτωχείαν) Chrysostom urges his hearers to pursue.

pass_b_english: That is why she was not the only woman of this kind; all the rest were too. For about a certain Persis he says, “She labored much for us” (Romans 16:12), and he admires Mary and Tryphaena for these very labors, because they toiled alongside the apostles and stripped for the same contests. And how is it that when writing to Timothy he says, “I do not permit a woman to teach or to have authority over a man” (1 Timothy 2:12)? This is when the husband is devout, possesses the same faith, and shares the same wisdom. But when he is an unbeliever and has gone astray, he does not deprive her of the authority of teaching. At any rate, when writing to the Corinthians he says, “And if a woman has an unbelieving husband, let her not leave him. For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?” (1 Corinthians 7:13, 16). And how would the believing woman save the unbelieving husband? By instructing him, clearly, and teaching him and leading him toward the faith, just as Priscilla did with Apollos. Besides, when he says, “I do not permit a woman to teach,” he is speaking about teaching on the platform, about public discourse, and about the kind that belongs to the priesthood; but he did not forbid private exhortation and counsel. For if it had been forbidden, he would not have praised this woman for doing it.

Let men hear, and let women hear these things too: the women, so that they may imitate their own kind and kinswoman; the men, so that they may not appear weaker than a woman. For what defense will we have, what pardon, when women display such eagerness and such discipline, while we are perpetually bound to the affairs of the world? Let rulers learn these things, and subjects, and priests, and those who hold the rank of the laity: the rulers, so that they may not admire the rich or chase after distinguished households, but seek virtue with poverty, and not be ashamed of the poorer among the brothers, nor pass by the tentmaker, the tanner, the purple-seller, and the bronze-worker to court those in positions of power. And the subjects, so that they may not think their circumstances are an obstacle to receiving holy people, but remembering the widow who received Elijah with only a handful of flour, and those who hosted Paul for two years, may they open their homes to those in need and hold all things in common with strangers.

Do not tell me, “You have no servants to wait on you.” For even if you have ten thousand, God commands you to harvest the fruit of hospitality through yourself. That is why Paul, speaking to a widow and commanding her to show hospitality, ordered her to do it not through others but through herself. For after saying, “If she has shown hospitality,” he added, “If she has washed the feet of the saints” (1 Timothy 5:10). He did not say, “If she spent money,” nor, “If she ordered her servants to do this,” but, “If she did this through herself.” That is why Abraham, though he had three hundred eighteen homeborn servants, ran to the herd himself, carried the calf, and performed all the other service himself, and made his wife a partner in the fruits of hospitality. That is why our Lord Jesus Christ was born in a manger, and after being born was raised in a house, and when he grew up had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), so that through all things he might teach you not to gape at the splendid affairs of this life, but to be a lover of simplicity everywhere, to pursue poverty, to flee abundance, and to be adorned from within.

problems.quote: one of their own race and kin
problems.why: 'Race' misleads; means 'of same nature/tribe' and 'kinswoman/relative', not racial category.

problems.quote: and those who hosted Paul for two years
problems.source_quote: τούτους, οἳ τὸν Παῦλον διετίαν ἐξένισαν
problems.why: Source says 'these' (people), referring to Priscilla and Aquila; English says 'those who hosted Paul,' losing the specific reference.
problems.fix: and those like Priscilla and Aquila, who hosted Paul for two years
problems.ruling: Source τούτους = 'these' specifically refers back to Priscilla/Aquila (Acts 18:2-3, 18, 26); 'those who' loses this specific reference, breaking the chain.

edits.old: one of their own race and kin
and those who hosted Paul for two years
edits.new: and these, who hosted Paul for two years

fixed: Changed 'one of their own race and kin' to 'their own kind and kinswoman': source 'τὴν ὁμόφυλον καὶ συγγενῆ' means 'of the same tribe/nature' and 'kinswoman/relative', not racial category.

Changed 'and those who hosted Paul for two years' to 'and these, who hosted Paul for two years': source 'τούτους, οἳ τὸν Παῦλον διετίαν ἐξένισαν' uses the demonstrative 'these', referring specifically to Priscilla and Aquila.

problems.quote: When the husband is devout, possesses the same faith, and shares the same wisdom.
problems.source_quote: Ὅταν καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ εὐλαβὴς ᾖ, καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν πίστιν κεκτημένος, καὶ τῆς αὐτῆς σοφίας μετέχων
problems.why: Source has this as a conditional clause ('whenever...'), but English drops the main clause explaining Paul's prohibition applies only when husband shares faith.
problems.fix: This is when the husband is devout, possesses the same faith, and shares the same wisdom.
problems.ruling: Greek Ὅταν...ᾖ sets up a conditional clause requiring a main clause; English drops it, losing the contrast with the following ὅταν δὲ clause and obscuring the argument structure.

edits.old: When the husband is devout, possesses the same faith, and shares the same wisdom.
edits.new: This is when the husband is devout, possesses the same faith, and shares the same wisdom.

fixed: Added 'This is' to make the conditional clause explicit, matching the source's 'Ὅταν' (whenever) and clarifying that Paul's prohibition applies only when the husband shares the faith.

problems.quote: and these, who hosted Paul for two years,
problems.source_quote: καὶ τούτους, οἳ τὸν Παῦλον διετίαν ἐξένισαν, τὰς οἰκίας διανοίγωσι τοῖς δεομένοις
problems.why: English drops main verb 'let them open their homes to those in need,' leaving 'and these' as a dangling fragment.
problems.fix: and those who hosted Paul for two years, may they open their homes to those in need
problems.ruling: English omits imperative verb διανοίγωσι ('let them open'), leaving dangling participial phrase.

edits.old: and these, who hosted Paul for two years, may open their homes to those in need
edits.new: and those who hosted Paul for two years, may they open their homes to those in need

fixed: The English did drop the main verb, leaving 'and these' as a dangling fragment. The source reads 'καὶ τούτους, οἳ τὸν Παῦλον διετίαν ἐξένισαν, τὰς οἰκίας διανοίγωσι τοῖς δεομένοις' — 'and those who hosted Paul for two years, may they open their homes to those in need.' I restored the verb and adjusted 'these' to 'those' to fit the optative construction.

last_rejected.quote: This is when the husband is devout
last_rejected.source_quote: Ὅταν καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ εὐλαβὴς ᾖ, καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν πίστιν κεκτημένος, καὶ τῆς αὐτῆς σοφίας μετέχων
last_rejected.why: English 'This is when' obscures that Paul is the speaker; the Greek shows Paul's condition for the prohibition, not Chrysostom's comment. The 'ὅταν' clause explains the scenario where Paul's command applies.
last_rejected.fix: He means: when the husband is devout, possesses the same faith, and shares the same wisdom.
last_rejected.ruling: Ὅταν clause is Chrysostom's explanation of when Paul's prohibition applies; 'This is when' captures this adequately.

last_rejected.quote: after being born was raised in a house
last_rejected.why: English adds 'after being born' which is not in the Greek; Greek says 'and in a house being born he is nourished/raised.' The participle 'τικτόμενος' is contemporaneous or causal, not sequential. 'After being born' changes the temporal logic.
last_rejected.fix: and being born in a house, is raised there
last_rejected.ruling: τικτόμενος τρέφεται: 'after being born was raised' is reasonable rendering; not a major meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: to be a lover of simplicity everywhere
last_rejected.why: 'Simplicity' is wrong; εὐτέλεια means 'cheapness, plainness, lack of luxury, humble circumstances'—'simplicity' in modern English suggests uncomplicatedness. Better: 'lowliness' or 'plain living' or 'frugality.' The sense is material modesty, not lack of complexity.
last_rejected.fix: to be a lover of plain living everywhere
last_rejected.ruling: εὐτελεία includes 'simplicity, plainness'; within normal range, not a major error.

last_rejected.why: Wait, these are present in English. Let me re-check... Yes they are present. No omission.
last_rejected.ruling: No omission; English includes 'purple-seller' and 'bronze-worker' as claimed.

last_rejected.quote: to court those in positions of power
last_rejected.why: 'Court' suggests romantic or social pursuit; θεραπεύω here means 'pay attention to, serve, flatter, cultivate' in the sense of currying favor. 'Court' is actually within range. But 'cultivate the powerful' or 'curry favor with' might be clearer. However, 'court' = 'pay attentions to, seek to please' is valid. Not a clear error.
last_rejected.ruling: θεραπεύω = 'serve, court, cultivate'; 'court those in power' is within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: Do not tell me, “You have no servants to wait on you.”
last_rejected.source_quote: Μὴ γάρ μοι τοῦτο εἴπῃς, ὅτι οἰκέτας οὐκ ἔχεις διακονουμένους.
last_rejected.why: Quoting indirect speech directly with "You" makes the listener say Chrysostom lacks servants, instead of excusing themselves for having none.
last_rejected.fix: Do not tell me that you have no servants to wait on you.
last_rejected.ruling: εἴπῃς ὅτι οἰκέτας οὐκ ἔχεις keeps the hearer as subject; quoted you still names the excuser, and the next verse clarifies.
